nameStory: The 'bunch-flowered' part of this daffodil's name comes from its habit of producing clusters of multiple flowers on a single stem, unlike many daffodils that have just one bloom per stalk. The scientific name 'tazetta' comes from the Italian word for 'little cup,' referring to the small corona (the cup-shaped center) of each flower.
description: Bunch-flowered Daffodil is a spring-blooming bulb that produces clusters of fragrant white flowers with bright yellow centers. Unlike the classic single-flowered daffodils, this species puts on quite a show with 4-8 flowers grouped together on each stem. The plant grows about 12-16 inches tall with narrow, strap-like leaves that emerge from the base. It's primarily grown as an ornamental garden plant and is especially popular for indoor forcing during winter.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Multiple small flowers (4-8) clustered on each stem, with pure white petals surrounding a bright yellow cup-shaped corona that's much smaller than the petals. The flowers have an intense, sweet fragrance that can perfume an entire room.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows from a brown, papery bulb sending up multiple flower stems, each topped with a bouquet-like cluster rather than a single bloom like most daffodils.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, strap-shaped leaves that are blue-green in color and emerge directly from the ground around the base of the flower stems. Feel smooth and somewhat thick, with parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Rarely produces fruit in New England's climate, but when it does, forms small green capsules that split open to reveal black seeds.

habitat: In New England, this is almost exclusively found in cultivated gardens, particularly in protected spots near foundations or in rock gardens where the bulbs can stay warmer. Very rarely escapes cultivation, preferring well-drained soil and sunny to partially shaded locations. Most commonly seen in coastal areas where winters are slightly milder.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in early to mid-spring, usually March to April, with the distinctive clusters of white and yellow blooms filling the air with intense fragrance. Leaves emerge alongside or just before the flowers.
seasonality.summer: Foliage remains green through early summer as the plant stores energy in its bulb, then gradually yellows and dies back completely by midsummer, leaving no trace above ground.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible growth above ground. This is the best time to plant new bulbs if you can find them.
seasonality.winter: Bulbs rest underground through the cold months, though popular cultivars like 'Ziva' are often forced indoors in pots for winter blooms, filling homes with their sweet scent.

funFact: This daffodil is so powerfully fragrant that just a few cut stems can perfume an entire house for days - in fact, the scent is sometimes considered overwhelming in small indoor spaces, earning it the nickname 'paperwhite' partly because people thought the pure white flowers looked too delicate to produce such an intense fragrance!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Paperwhite (Narcissus papyraceus), which is extremely similar and sometimes considered the same species. Paperwhites tend to have pure white coronas (cups) while bunch-flowered daffodils typically have yellow ones - remember 'yellow cup = tazetta group.'
contextualKnowledge: Many garden centers sell what they call 'paperwhites' for indoor forcing, but these are often actually bunch-flowered daffodils or very closely related forms. The taxonomy of this group is quite confused, with botanists still debating whether some forms are separate species or just varieties of the same plant.
compareHints: Unlike wild daffodil which has one large flower per stem, this species always has multiple smaller flowers clustered together. Compared to Poet's Narcissus, the corona (cup) is much larger relative to the petals, and the fragrance is far more intense. Angel's-tears has even smaller flowers that hang downward, while this species holds its flower clusters upright and proud.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the familiar yellow trumpet daffodils (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) that bloom earlier, poet's narcissus has pure white petals and a flat, small center rather than a large trumpet.

Wild daffodil differs from its Narcissus relatives by having pale yellow petals rather than the pure white of Poet's Narcissus or Paperwhite, and produces single flowers rather than the clusters seen in Bunch-flowered Daffodil.

Unlike other daffodils in New England, the hoop-petticoat has an enormous corona that completely dominates tiny, thread-like petals - the exact opposite of poet's narcissus which has huge white petals and a tiny orange cup.
Unlike other New England daffodils that bloom singly in spring with thick, substantial petals, paperwhite produces clusters of smaller flowers with distinctively thin, translucent petals.
Angel's-tears differs from other New England daffodils by its tiny size, pure white color, and distinctly drooping flowers.
